---
title: "Visuals, humour and credit"
last-reviewed: "2026-08-29"
---

The handbook can be serious without sounding solemn on every page. A well-placed cartoon, visual analogy or familiar research frustration can help a reader remember an idea. The joke must serve the teaching point, not turn the handbook into a gallery of borrowed internet culture.

There is no image quota. A page can use an original illustration, a properly cleared third-party work, a link to an external work, or no visual at all. If an image does not sharpen the lesson, the page is better without it.

## What we can embed

The preferred order is:

1. **Original diagrams and illustrations.** These can be created by a human contributor or produced with disclosed AI assistance under human editorial direction.
2. **Openly licensed or public-domain material.** The licence on the individual work must permit this use. The creator, source, licence and any changes are recorded.
3. **A link to the original work.** If a meme, comic or image is relevant but its reuse rights are unclear, link to the creator's page rather than copying the image into the handbook.

A familiar meme setup can inspire a new joke, but the published image must still be our own. We can draw an original researcher facing two awkward choices, enjoying a small victory or watching a plan meet reality. We do not trace, closely recreate or relabel the photograph, film frame, comic panel, character or exact composition of an existing meme template.

Wikimedia Commons notes that files can carry different reuse and attribution conditions, so the status of each file must be checked on its own description page [@wikimedia-commons-reuse]. Creative Commons likewise recommends making the applicable licence, creator and source easy to identify [@creative-commons-licensing].

## What we will not embed

- a recognisable commercial meme template, cartoon character or comic panel without permission or a clear reuse licence;
- an image copied from a meme-aggregation site merely because it includes a creator's name;
- a watermarked stock image or an image whose source cannot be traced;
- a visual that exposes a participant, student, colleague, private document or research setting without appropriate authority;
- humour about harm, misconduct, bullying, discrimination, serious wellbeing concerns, examination failure or another person's vulnerability; or
- an image that relies on stereotypes, humiliation or inaccessible text to make its point.

Giving credit does not cure a missing licence. Attribution and permission are separate checks.

For example, [PHD Comics asks people to obtain permission before reproducing its comics](https://phdcomics.com/about.php). We will identify a useful strip first, request permission for that exact use and wait for written approval before embedding it. Until then, a link is the most the handbook will provide.

## The credit line

Every content image must have useful alternative text. A third-party image also needs a visible credit line that records:

- title or short description;
- creator or rightsholder;
- direct source link;
- exact licence and licence link;
- whether the image was cropped, annotated, translated or otherwise changed;
- the date its reuse status was checked; and
- whether it is excluded from the handbook's general CC BY 4.0 licence.

An AI-assisted original uses this pattern:

> Original illustration created for *The Handbook for the Recently Enrolled* with human editorial direction and AI-assisted production. See the visual-assets register for provenance and reuse information.

## The visual-assets register

The current cover is an original AI-assisted illustration made for this project, with two researchers approaching an imagined library. Its worn-book appearance draws on vintage manuals; the illustration is not taken from a film. The project offers it under CC BY 4.0 where copyright subsists.

The project records each embedded image in the [`visual-assets register`](https://github.com/hareshsuppiah/handbook-for-the-recently-enrolled/blob/main/research/visual-assets-register.csv). This makes image source, licence, credit, alternative text and placement reviewable before publication.

Review every visual for its teaching purpose, accuracy, safety, accessibility, rights and tone. A funny image that fails one of those checks does not go in.
